candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: The freedom relevant to moral responsibility is compatible with determinism and consists in ordinary responsible agency rather than libertarian metaphysics.
candidates.attributionBasis: The microphone handoff identifies Dennett, and the uninterrupted turn continues until Harris explicitly begins responding.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This establishes the compatibilist answer to the motion by separating responsibility-grounding freedom from indeterministic or agent-causal freedom.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's earlier portrayal of Dennett's compatibilism as quasi-theological and as failing to acknowledge that free will is unreal.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett stresses extensive agreement about rejecting libertarianism, then locates valuable freedom in competent, uncoerced agency that supports contracts, responsibility, and justified punishment.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism legitimately preserves a naturalistic meaning of free will by refining inherited concepts instead of treating their magical interpretations as definitive.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris invites Dennett to define compatibilism, after which Dennett speaks continuously until Harris poses his objection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the conceptual methodology behind Dennett's position and explains why rejecting a magical definition need not require abandoning free-will language.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that compatibilism resembles theology and does not identify a serious form of free will.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett treats disputes over whether consciousness or free will exists as partly diplomatic choices between eliminating a misleading concept and retaining a purified naturalistic version.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism risks changing the subject because purifying a concept can discard features that are indispensable to what people mean by free will.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn begins as a direct objection to Dennett's preceding account and ends when Dennett immediately answers it.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This frames Harris's principal conceptual objection: the compatibilist phenomenon may be real while failing to answer the original free-will concern.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that free will can truthfully be said to exist once its magical and traditional baggage is removed.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris distinguishes scientifically explaining a real phenomenon from redefining it so extensively that the supposedly preserved concept no longer addresses its core concern.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Free will is the reasons-responsive competence to control an agent's many practical degrees of freedom, and this capacity—not indeterminism—grounds responsibility.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett directly takes up Harris's objection and retains the microphone throughout the extended engineering and responsible-agent account.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the central positive compatibilist model, connecting freedom, rational control, self-control, absence of usurpation, and moral responsibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's objection that compatibilism merely changes the subject by eliminating the concept's essential incompatibilist feature.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett rejects a sharp line between clarification and subject change, then models freedom through controllable capacities, responsiveness to reasons, and the distinction between competent agents and constrained or controlled ones.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: The enduring free-will problem concerns first-person authorship and the ability to do otherwise, neither of which is supported by determinism or indeterminism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris begins after acknowledging Dennett's account and speaks continuously through a sustained first-person analysis of agency.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This identifies the experiential and metaphysical target Harris believes compatibilism misses and gives his direct argument against conscious authorship.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's account of free will as reasons-responsive control that can be fully distinguished within either a deterministic or indeterministic world.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris separates first-person experience from third-person functional description, denies that an exact replay permits another choice, and argues that thoughts simply arise from unconscious processes.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism preserves real capacities but calls them free will in the way one might preserve Sicily while abandoning the fictional features that made Atlantis the subject of interest.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same Harris turn explicitly introduces an analogy from his prior response and develops it until Dennett answers.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The analogy sharpens the subject-changing objection by conceding compatibilist facts while denying that they answer the motivating first-person claim.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's proposal to retain free-will language for naturalistic capacities after removing libertarian and magical commitments.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris compares rejecting libertarian freedom while retaining compatibilist agency to rejecting mythical Atlantis while redirecting attention to a real island sharing peripheral features.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: A nonmagical form of free will preserves the responsibility distinctions people need, while the experience of deciding requires treating some possibilities as open without requiring absolute metaphysical openness.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly reconstructs Harris's position and then delivers a continuous response about naturalistic responsibility and deliberation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly answers both the subject-changing charge and the experiential challenge by arguing that practical agency supplies the freedom worth preserving.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's Atlantis analogy and his claim that people's felt ability to do otherwise is the indispensable feature compatibilism abandons.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett concedes that magical freedom does not exist but argues that naturalistic agency retains daily responsibility practices and that deliberation necessarily represents alternatives as unsettled.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: An agent can meaningfully have been able to do otherwise when a small variation would produce another choice, even if the decision process itself is deterministic.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett continues the same uninterrupted turn, using a deterministic chess program to clarify counterfactual ability and design competence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This provides a concrete compatibilist analysis of alternative possibilities and separates unlucky outcomes from defects in an agent's decision-making design.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's exact-replay standard under which an agent could not have done otherwise unless the identical prior state produced a different result.

candidates.contextSummary: A deterministic chess program can lose after one pseudo-random result while remaining well designed; nearby variations support an ordinary counterfactual sense in which it could have chosen differently.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Dependence of major life choices on minute neural differences is deeply subversive of ordinary personhood because it makes the universe, rather than a conscious self, control the outcome.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris takes the microphone with an explicit concession followed by a sustained objection, ending when Dennett begins his answer.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This explains why accepting compatibilist counterfactuals does not resolve Harris's concern: causal sensitivity itself revives the loss-of-authorship problem.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's deterministic chess example and claim that tiny variations can justify saying a well-designed agent could have acted otherwise.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris accepts the functional analysis but argues that tiny neurophysiological contingencies controlling transformative choices conflict with how people experience themselves as authors of their lives.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Neither absolute indeterminacy nor sensitivity to tiny changes defeats freedom: close decisions may flip under small variations, while reason-dominated decisions require much larger changes.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly answers Harris's immediately preceding objection and continues beyond the owned core through the available boundary context.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This distinguishes genuine toss-ups from decisions settled by reasons and argues that determination can express, rather than negate, responsible agency.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that minute physical contingencies behind consequential choices restore marionette-like control by the universe and undermine personhood.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett calls absolute undetermination irrelevant, distinguishes finely balanced choices from strongly reason-governed ones, and begins using a determined yet responsibility-affirming decision as a counterexample.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Chance can settle genuinely balanced decisions without undermining responsibility, while strongly reason-supported decisions remain robust against small physical variations.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn continues Dennett's compatibilist response from the lookbehind and ends at Harris's explicit transition into disagreement.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This establishes the compatibilist distinction between unavoidable local luck and the reasons-responsive control sufficient for freedom and responsibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that microscopic causal differences can redirect important choices and expose the absence of authorship.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett treats borderline choices as possible toss-ups, rejects libertarian indeterminacy, and argues that accepting responsibility never requires complete control over every element of deliberation.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Although undetermined choices would not be free, tiny unchosen neural differences can still determine consequential actions and radically alter a life.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker announces disagreement with Dennett, develops Harris's characteristic luck argument, and is answered directly in the following turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move accepts the critique of libertarianism while challenging the claim that consequential causal divergence occurs only in harmlessly balanced decisions.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's position that microscopic variation matters chiefly in genuine toss-ups and does not threaten responsible agency.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris agrees that randomness cannot supply authorship but argues that small differences in sleep or neural state can decide whether someone performs a life-changing act.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Complete causal understanding would make ordinary wrongdoing resemble the exculpatory brain-tumor case because no agent authors the decisive neural conditions.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly contrasts Harris's eliminativist account with Dennett's redefinition and introduces Harris's published Charles Whitman argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly advances the core no-libertarian-free-will case by extending causal non-authorship from exceptional pathology to every human action.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that practical responsibility survives luck because agents can exercise differing degrees of self-control.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris distinguishes their rival responses to incoherent libertarian freedom, then argues from Charles Whitman's tumor to the exculpatory force of complete neurophysiological explanation.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Being causally wired is not equivalent to being impaired, so exceptional neurological disability cannot justify treating every normally capable agent as exculpated.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker immediately answers the brain-tumors-all-the-way-down formulation and articulates Dennett's distinction between capable and disabled agents.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response protects compatibilist responsibility by denying that universal causation erases the functional capacity distinction on which accountability rests.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's argument that complete neurophysiology makes all conduct exculpatory in the same sense as Charles Whitman's tumor.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett says neuroscience shows that people are wired, not universally wired wrongly, and maintains a revisable but durable boundary between adequate agency and disabling impairment.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Differences in capacity remain real, but genes, upbringing, environment, and each persuasive input are unchosen, making ultimate blame unjustified while pragmatic accountability remains useful.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker concedes Dennett's capacity distinctions, then restates Harris's causal luck argument through upbringing, persuasion, Saddam Hussein, and punishment.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies Harris's main reconciliation of causal non-authorship with contracts, restraint, and behavior-shaping sanctions rather than ultimate desert.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's assertion that normally functioning people are sufficiently able to be responsible despite universal causal wiring.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris argues that greater information makes ordinary agents resemble exculpated cases, illustrates this through an unlucky childhood, and retains responsibility only for beneficial practical effects.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Control consists in responding competently to factors one did not choose, and moral education enables people to become and maintain practically responsible self-controlling agents.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker labels a flaw in Harris's examples, uses Dennett's sailor-control analogy, and develops the compatibilist role of moral education and self-maintenance.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This positively defines compatibilist control and explains how causally formed people acquire autonomy, duties of self-regulation, and corresponding social freedoms.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's contention that unchosen genes and environment eliminate genuine control and reduce responsibility to pragmatic behavior management.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett compares agency to steering amid uncontrollable wind, argues that total causal independence is irrelevant, and links moral formation and continued self-control to practical responsibility.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: A rare lapse by the most competent agent is simultaneously the strongest occasion for blame and the weakest expression of that agent's settled character, revealing luck's role.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker first concedes practical capacity distinctions and then presents Harris's Tiger Woods competence-and-luck paradox for Dennett to answer.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The paradox challenges the inference from high competence to deeper authorship by arguing that anomalous failures are especially unrepresentative and adventitious.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that developed competence and reliable self-control ground an adult's practical responsibility for maintaining conduct.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris accepts reasons-responsive differences among agents but argues that an expert's exceptionally unlikely failure says least about the expert and most clearly reflects bad luck.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Greater competence creates greater reliance-based obligations, and anomalous failure may expose correctable prior conduct rather than a paradoxical absence of responsibility.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker welcomes the example, substitutes a moral case, rejects the alleged paradox, and answers with obligation, reliance, and self-correction considerations.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This counters the competence paradox by grounding heightened responsibility in undertaken expectations and by treating causal diagnosis as a route to improved control.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that a highly competent person's rare lapse is maximally blameworthy yet minimally expressive of free agency.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett argues that trusted competent agents assume special obligations, that others rely on them, and that investigating antecedents can identify failures they can subsequently correct.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Tracing an anomalous lapse to earlier conduct merely uncovers further unchosen causes, while accountability and public safety can be preserved without belief in ultimate self-authorship.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly says Dennett missed the first-person point, extends Harris's regress of causes, and offers a pragmatic alternative to ultimate authorship.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move answers causal self-correction while presenting Harris's central proposal that social accountability need not depend on metaphysical authorship.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's argument that competent agents undertake obligations and can diagnose antecedent failures to improve their future self-control.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris says a radical deviation from internalized norms is unusually unrepresentative, pushes every proposed prior explanation back into causal luck, and preserves contracts and confinement pragmatically.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Limited self-authorship assembled from inherited materials is enough for moral agency, so responsible agents should accept deserved consequences despite pervasive luck.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn directly distinguishes absolute from ordinary self-authorship and continues coherently through the locked lookahead before Harris resumes at event 1688.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This crystallizes the compatibilist conclusion that finite, socially embedded self-construction and accountability remain meaningful without absolute causal authorship.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's position that nobody truly authors themselves and that accountability should therefore rest only on pragmatic social needs.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett concedes limits and luck but maintains that people partly construct themselves, participate in shared moral practices, and cannot excuse a failure merely as cosmic misfortune.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Practical rules may treat an agent as responsible, but fuller causal knowledge would show that luck and prior causes, rather than genuine authorship, produced the particular failure.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage directly continues Harris's recurring causal-luck argument and is followed by Dennett explicitly challenging its demand for absolute responsibility.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This separates the practical usefulness of responsibility practices from the deeper claim that an individual truly authored the action, a central distinction in Harris's case.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that responsible agents should accept accountability despite the pervasive role of luck in producing their conduct.

candidates.contextSummary: Using a missed athletic performance, Harris argues that institutions may reasonably employ responsibility heuristics even though a complete causal account would deny ultimate responsibility for the event.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Rejecting absolute responsibility does not eliminate ordinary responsibility, whose point is a pragmatic and consequentialist system of reasonable expectations, excuses, and enforceable social rules.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly accuses Harris of reverting to absolute responsibility and develops Dennett's characteristic consequentialist account of law and responsibility.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The passage states the core compatibilist position that responsibility worth preserving is a practical social achievement rather than metaphysical self-creation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's contention that a causally determined failure makes the actor not genuinely responsible and leaves only a pragmatic heuristic.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett argues that law properly draws pragmatic lines shaped by human capacities, excusing some conditions while preserving expectations and respect for a socially valuable legal order.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: If severe antisocial behavior became causally understood and reliably curable, treatment would replace retributive punishment and expose apparent evil as a condition rather than self-authored wickedness.
candidates.attributionBasis: The thought experiment extends Harris's earlier Charles Whitman reasoning and receives Dennett's immediate acknowledgment that the proposed cure would be exculpatory.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The cure scenario tests whether increased causal knowledge systematically erodes desert-based blame, directly supporting Harris's challenge to ultimate moral responsibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's pragmatic defense of responsibility practices and legal boundaries despite luck, causation, and the absence of absolute self-authorship.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris imagines a maximally remorseless offender transformed by a reliable intervention, arguing that successful causal treatment would make retribution seem inappropriate and medically obsolete.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Even if antisocial dispositions were diagnosable and curable, credible punishment would remain necessary because agents anticipate sanctions and shared enforcement sustains lawful cooperation.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage is an explicit rebuttal to the cure scenario and develops Dennett's familiar analogy between legal penalties and rule-governed sports.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It supplies the systemic compatibilist justification for responsibility: sanctions shape deliberation and preserve mutually understood expectations beyond rehabilitation of one offender.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that identifying and curing a Madoff-like causal syndrome would transform culpable wrongdoing into an exculpatory medical condition.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett argues that knowledge of treatment would itself alter incentives, while dependable penalties deter wrongdoing and maintain the common expectations required by games, law, and moral life.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Deterrence may justify punishment pragmatically, yet complete causal knowledge would still dissolve personal authorship, and advance neural prediction would reveal the agent's felt control as illusory.
candidates.attributionBasis: The speaker accepts deterrence before returning to Harris's characteristic distinction between social utility, causal truth, and first-person authorship.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This passage directly joins the debate's moral-responsibility and conscious-agency strands by conceding social management while denying that it establishes genuine authorship.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's argument that dependable penalties preserve cooperation, deter dispositionally dangerous people, and thereby ground meaningful responsibility.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris distinguishes the practical design of justice from what agents truly are, then argues that sufficiently detailed prediction of thought and action would shatter the subjective sense of authorship.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Neuroscientific decoding does not yet provide real-time foreknowledge, and prediction that interacts with its subject faces principled self-referential limits, so current findings do not establish the proposed authorship-destroying scenario.

candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument challenges a key empirical and conceptual premise of Harris's prediction thought experiment, limiting its force against conscious agency and authorship.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that neuroscience could know each thought and action before the subject does and thereby expose conscious authorship as an illusion.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett distinguishes retrospective data analysis from genuine live prediction and adds that an interacting predictor must include its own behavior, creating theoretical limits on complete forecasts.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: If a complete record of a person's words could be produced before conscious awareness, that foreknowledge would undermine free will because consciousness enters too late to originate the unfolding action.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage sharpens Harris's immediately preceding neural-prediction argument and is followed by Dennett identifying confusions in the proposed example.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The thought experiment isolates Harris's central first-person objection: prior determination and preconscious neural formation conflict with the experience of consciously originating action.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's objection that present experiments lack real-time predictive power and that an interacting complete predictor encounters self-referential limits.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris asks the listener to imagine an advance transcript of the conversation and argues that even short-lag mind reading would show conscious awareness following rather than directing production.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Authorship does not require conscious control of every microscopic generative step; agents author actions through practiced capacities, advance planning, and temporally extended macro-level control.
candidates.attributionBasis: The extended response directly challenges Harris's prediction standard and uses Dennett's examples of arithmetic, artistic creation, athletics, and improvisation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This provides the central compatibilist model of conscious agency, relocating control from instantaneous awareness of neural details to reasons-responsive, trained, extended organization.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's argument that preconscious generation and advance prediction show consciousness arriving too late for a person to count as the author.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett argues that predictable competence is not unfree and that artists and athletes remain authors when deliberate plans recruit trained processes whose fine-grained outputs are not consciously selected.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism preserves a third-person notion of competence but still forfeits the first-person freedom people value, because under identical conditions the agent could not genuinely have acted otherwise.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage explicitly contrasts first- and third-person perspectives, identifies the disagreement with compatibilism, and states Harris's conclusion about alternatives.
candidates.loadBearingReason: It identifies the alleged mismatch between Dennett's functional freedom and the psychologically important libertarian capacity that Harris argues ordinary people believe they possess.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that macro-level planning and trained control are sufficient for conscious authorship despite unconscious generation of particular movements or ideas.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris says both speakers reject libertarian metaphysics but differ over the loss involved: Dennett discounts alternative possibilities, whereas Harris treats their falsity as psychologically consequential.

candidates.proposition: An agent could have done otherwise in the relevant sense when possessing a real competence for multiple responses; demanding atom-for-atom replay mistakes deterministic identity for practical causal possibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's assertion that both speakers ultimately agree no one could have done otherwise, with compatibilism merely minimizing the importance of that loss.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett grounds alternative possibility in an agent's range of abilities and maintains that microscopic replication is irrelevant to the causal distinctions used in ordinary deliberation and action.

candidates.proposition: The ordinary felt sense of libertarian authorship presumes ultimate control, and sufficiently predictive neuroimaging would undermine that sense by revealing decisions before conscious awareness.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's earlier position that deterministic causal processes can still support meaningful alternatives and the freedom worth wanting.

candidates.contextSummary: Following discussion of randomness and ultimate causal ownership, Harris argues that advance prediction of deliberation would directly threaten people's experienced authorship of creative and voluntary conduct.

candidates.proposition: Deterministic chaos is not an inferior substitute for quantum indeterminacy in the free-will debate because the physical distinction between them produces no difference in moral responsibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's characterization of a coin flip as merely a surrogate for genuine randomness and his broader concern that deterministic causation defeats authentic authorship.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett responds to Harris's distinction between chaotic unpredictability and true randomness by denying that the distinction changes any morally relevant feature of agency.

candidates.proposition: Because indeterminism adds nothing morally relevant, people do not need libertarian freedom; the forms of freedom genuinely worth wanting remain fully compatible with determinism.
